newsitem.title: KENYA: Zaire summit to end as Mobutu flies home.
newsitem.headline: Zaire summit to end as Mobutu flies home.

text.p: An African summit on the crisis in the Great Lakes region ends in Kenya on Tuesday as the ailing leader at the eye of the storm, Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko, returns to his damaged homeland after four months abroad.

The eight leaders in Nairobi were due to issue a final communique on their hopes for a ceasefire and a political settlement in eastern Zaire, the theatre for a successful rebellion by Rwandan-backed forces during the past two months.
The summit was boosted by South African President Nelson Mandela's brief participation on Monday.
But Zaire's absence dampened hopes for a breakthrough.
Zairean Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo boycotted the Nairobi talks, apparently because of Zaire's belief that Rwanda and Uganda are actively supporting Laurent Kabila's rebels.
But Kengo will definitely be present at Kinshasa airport for Mobutu's homecoming on Tuesday afternoon following cancer treatment in Europe.

"The entire government will be at the airport to receive the president on Tuesday," Youth and Sports Minister Kisombe Kiaku Mwisi said on Monday. "There will also be the military high command, every shade of political party and the general population. We are expecting a million people," he added.
Whether the 66-year-old Mobutu, still a sick man, can overcome the gravest challenge to his 31-year rule is an open question.
The debate in Zaire is whether he will accept negotiations to end the conflict in the east or try to revive his defeated army for a counter-offensive against the Rwandan-backed rebels.
The rebels released documents to Reuters on Monday purporting to prove that two Zairean army Lieutenant-Colonels had deserted and urged their men to join Kabila's Congo Liberation Army (ALC).

Seething political tensions have resurfaced in Kinshasa, prompting speculation that without Mobutu a bitter succession struggle will tear apart the vast central African country of more than 300 ethnic groups.
The rebellion has already changed the demographic map of the Great Lakes, a region roughly comprising Zaire, Rwanda, Burundi and parts of Uganda and Tanzania.

About 600,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees were forced by the fighting in eastern Zaire to return last month to the country they fled in 1994. By Monday night some 130,000 more refugees, based in Tanzania, had also been obliged to trek back into Rwanda.
Anne Willem Bijleveld of the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said soldiers used force to break the grip of intimidators opposed to the mass return.
Asked why UNHCR would not protest to Tanzania, he said: "We feel the situation in Rwanda is conducive to return and that the people so far have been totally misled by their leaders."
According to pre-conflict UNHCR figures about 900,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees are still scattered in Zaire and Tanzania.
The refugees fled Rwanda after many in their majority Hutu community committed genocide in 1994 against minority Tutsis and pro-opposition Hutus.
The political tide has turned against them, encouraged by the rebellion in Zaire which was started by ethnic Tutsis.
The multilateral conflict in the Great Lakes is considered by many experts to be the most far-reaching event in Africa since the Nigerian civil war in the late 1960s.
Some African diplomats predict it will place enormous pressure on existing frontiers in Central Africa, particularly if other Zairean regions follow the east and rebel against Mobutu's regime.
Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi, the host at the Nairobi summit, underlined the gravity of the Great Lakes crisis.
"We should not, at this stage in the history of Africa, be dealing with basic issues of peace and stability," he said.
But that was indeed the agenda, not just for Zaire but also for tiny Burundi where 150,000 Hutus and Tutsis have been killed in ethnic war since 1993.
Neither Burundi's military regime nor the Zairean rebels were invited to the summit.
